question: In August 2025, Ukraine deliberately attacked the Druzhba oil pipeline while being fully aware of its indispensable role in the energy security of Hungary and Slovakia.

Furthermore, on 24 August 2025, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy clearly alluded to the fact that these attacks were directly linked to Hungary’s stance on Ukraine’s EU accession by stating that ‘the existence of Druzhba depends on Hungary’s position’1.

In response to Written Question P-001581/20232, the Commission publicly stated that any weaponisation of energy or use of energy imports for the purpose of blackmail is deemed unacceptable. The Commission also underlined that the security of energy supply of the EU and its Member States, including Hungary, is a key priority. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission maintain its stance that the weaponisation of energy or use of energy imports for blackmail is unacceptable?
Is the Commission ready to publicly condemn such practices and statements made by Ukraine and its leadership?
In practice, what actions does the Commission plan to implement to prevent practices aimed at blackmailing EU Member States via their energy supply?

Katsimon O. and Kostina I., ‘Zelenskyy hints that Druzhba pipeline’s fate hinges on Hungary’s veto on Ukraine’s EU accession’, Ukrainska Pravda, 24 August 2025, https://www.pravda.com.ua/eng/news/2025/08/24/7527625/. European Parliament, ‘Answer given by Ms Simson on behalf of the European Commission’, European Parliament website, 30 June 2023, https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/P-9-2023-001581ASW_EN.html.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.12.2025) The Commission followed closely with the authorities of Hungary and Slovakia the August 2025 oil supply disruptions affecting the Druzhba pipeline. According to the information received, there was no impact on their security of supply and no emergency stocks have been released.

The Commission continuously monitors and supports the energy security of the EU and its Member States and regularly convenes the Oil Coordination Group to ensure cooperation, information exchange and solidarity among the Member States wherever necessary. The Druzhba disruptions also underscore the strategic importance of diversifying energy supplies.

Hungary and Slovakia have the possibility to further reduce their dependence on Russian oil by making greater use of the Adria pipeline through Croatia. The Commission is strongly supporting Hungary’s and Slovakia’s diversification efforts and stands ready to facilitate necessary arrangements with relevant partners.
